written_by: Claude (Anthropic), the AI assistant used to build this project
how: Written from each record's stored PSI text and from this site's own table profiles and curator report. Checked at every build by pipeline/zgf/briefs.py: a brief is dropped if it holds a number the record does not hold, a verdict, or names a record that is not there.

PSI-10.what: Spherical gas flames of ethylene and methane on the station, burned to find where soot begins as flow, dilution and pressure change.
PSI-10.why: Its 327 rows state oxygen and pressure for each flame, and NASA's own flame-temperature column in them is what this site checks its model against.

PSI-20.what: A porous burner that stands in for a burning solid, used to find when a flame survives in still air in free fall.
PSI-20.why: NASA's record says steady burning was seen with no air flow at all, which bears directly on the belief that stopping ventilation puts a fire out.

PSI-21.what: Weak coflow flames of methane and ethylene, measured for shape, lift-off, temperature and extinction as velocity and dilution change.
PSI-21.why: It is benchmark data for flame models rather than a fire-safety test. The table lists test conditions, not outcomes for materials.

PSI-22.what: Gas flames in an electric field, studied for ion current, soot and lifted flames near their limit.
PSI-22.why: NASA's record says it was not run for a space application. It ranks low for a habitat and is kept so that the set is complete.

PSI-23.what: Spherical diffusion flames, with and without soot, measured to test models of transport and chemistry.
PSI-23.why: Useful for checking models. Its atmosphere column carries a spreadsheet fill error, which the curator report flags.

PSI-25.what: Solid fuels burned in a small flow duct on the station, to study ignition, flame spread and extinction in slow forced air.
PSI-25.why: This is the experiment behind the fan question. Its 129 rows record flow, oxygen and gas readings, but no column says whether each flame went out.

PSI-26.what: The earlier series of solid-fuel burns in the station's glovebox, begun to connect NASA's ground flammability test with burning in free fall.
PSI-26.why: Its 122 rows list samples and materials. Few test conditions vary in the table, so it supports comparison less than BASS-II does.

PSI-39.what: Droplets of n-dodecane and its mixtures burned at 0.25 to 5 atm, to see when a cool flame follows the hot one.
PSI-39.why: Its 87 rows state oxygen, pressure and diluent, so they sit on the atmosphere map. Cool flames here concern fuel droplets, not cabin materials.

PSI-47.what: A test of a commercial particle counter on the station, flown to reduce the risk for the smoke experiment SAME.
PSI-47.why: It asked whether the counter works without gravity: a step towards smoke detection for long missions. Its table has 2 rows.

PSI-60.what: A ground study that reanalysed SPICE flame images to derive temperature and soot at Earth gravity and in free fall.
PSI-60.why: It shows PSI data being reused by other researchers. It has no experimental table of its own.

PSI-62.what: A modelling study of flame spread along the direction of the air flow in free fall.
PSI-62.why: NASA's record says it yields tools for screening the flammability limits of new materials. It has no experimental table.

PSI-68.what: Droplet burns that extend FLEX to fuels and conditions closer to real combustors, including two-component droplets.
PSI-68.why: Its table has 8 rows that list the fuels. It says what was burned, not how each test ended.

PSI-69.what: Fuel droplets burned on the station to map flammability limits and to measure how well gas suppressants such as CO2 and helium work.
PSI-69.why: The richest table for a habitat designer: 274 rows with oxygen, pressure, diluent and how each test ended.

PSI-98.what: A large fire lit on purpose inside an uncrewed cargo vehicle, to see how fast it grows in free fall.
PSI-98.why: One of the few tests at the scale of a real cabin fire. Its record carries the dates and proposal title of another experiment, which the curator report flags.

PSI-99.what: Material samples burned in a cargo vehicle, to compare flammability limits in free fall with NASA's ground screening test.
PSI-99.why: Its 15 rows give material, thickness, ignition and burn length. Oxygen is recorded; pressure is not.

PSI-100.what: The third large burn in a cargo vehicle, asking again how fast a big fire grows in free fall.
PSI-100.why: Its table has 2 rows. The value is the scale of the fire, not the number of tests.

PSI-101.what: A reflight that measured how large smoke particles grow in free fall, for several sample types and air speeds.
PSI-101.why: Smoke detectors sense particles, so particle size decides what an alarm can see. Its 109 rows give sample, inlet velocity and ageing time.

PSI-102.what: A measurement of how large smoke particles grow in free fall, tied to how the smoke was made and moved.
PSI-102.why: NASA's record names the goal: technology for an advanced fire detector for long missions.

PSI-106.what: Small gas jet flames, studied for what holds a flame at its base and when it lifts off the burner.
PSI-106.why: Mostly a test of flame models. Its 12 rows list fuels.

PSI-107.what: Gas jet flames in a flow of air, burned to find the smoke point under different nozzles and flow rates.
PSI-107.why: The largest table in scope: 469 rows of fuel, nozzle and flow. Soot matters to a habitat twice, for detection and for radiant heat.

PSI-115.what: A simulation study of how gravity changes the growth of smoke from heated materials.
PSI-115.why: It explains why smoke in free fall differs from smoke on Earth, which is the detector's problem. It has no experimental table.

PSI-117.what: A ground study that used FLEX flight data to see how heating and drift change the fate of a droplet's cool flame.
PSI-117.why: Its files mix experiment and simulation, so this site does not pool them. It has no experimental table.

PSI-142.what: Simulations and ground experiments, built on FLEX data, to chart where cool flames can exist.
PSI-142.why: Its table of 8 rows points to published figures rather than to tests.

PSI-159.what: Gas flames of propane, butane and pentane on the station, burned to find when a cool flame appears.
PSI-159.why: Its 333 rows state oxygen and pressure. Checking them against this site's model showed that NASA's flame-temperature column is reproduced only at one atmosphere.
